analysis.one_liner: Makes it illegal to gouge prices on gasoline during declared energy emergencies, enforced by the FTC with big penalties.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Commerce Committee until the 118th Congress ended, so no federal gasoline anti-gouging law was created.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal offense to charge unconscionably excessive prices for gasoline during an energy crisis declared by the President. The President could proclaim a crisis lasting 30 days at a time, renewable, covering any geographic area. During such a crisis, a seller who jacks up prices far above what they charged beforehand or what competitors charge could face civil penalties of up to three times the extra profits or $100 million, criminal fines up to $500 million, and lawsuits from state attorneys general. The FTC was to focus enforcement on companies with more than $10 billion a year in fuel sales. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Motorists and other fuel buyers would benefit during price spikes tied to wars, hurricanes, or refinery outages, when gasoline is a necessity and drivers have no choice but to fill up. Households that can least absorb a $6-a-gallon week would be protected from sellers boosting prices far above their own prior levels or competitors' prices, and state attorneys general could sue on their behalf.

how_it_helps.text: During a President-declared energy emergency, it becomes illegal to sell gasoline at prices that are unconscionably excessive and take unfair advantage of the crisis.

Sellers can face civil penalties of up to three times the profits gained or $100 million, plus criminal fines up to $500 million, with the FTC told to prioritize enforcement against companies with over $10 billion in annual fuel sales.
State attorneys general can sue on behalf of their residents, and the bill does not override any state law.

analysis.who_pays: Oil refiners, wholesalers, and gas stations, which would face penalties of up to three times excess profits or $100 million per violation, plus criminal fines up to $500 million, if they profit unreasonably during a declared emergency. Enforcement priority falls on the largest companies, those with over $10 billion in annual fuel sales.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big oil companies and gas sellers

drawbacks.text: The bill gives the President broad discretion to declare a crisis and renew 30-day prohibitions repeatedly, which critics would say gives too much pricing authority to whoever holds the office.

Standards like 'unconscionably excessive' and 'unfair advantage' are fuzzy, and oil companies argue that anti-gouging rules can worsen shortages by discouraging sellers from raising prices to ration scarce supply or bring in fuel from elsewhere.

Penalties are very large — up to triple the profits gained or $100 million per violation, plus possible criminal fines up to $500 million — which industry would call disproportionate, even if applied only during declared emergencies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — protecting drivers from price spikes they cannot avoid when fuel is a necessity — is large at the moment of an emergency, and it is targeted to emergencies only, so it does not control prices in normal times. The costs are real but manageable: companies would face new compliance and enforcement risk, and vague terms like "unconscionably excessive" could produce uneven enforcement or deter some price adjustments. On balance the design is reasonable and the ordinary-person benefit outweighs the industry cost. Its fatal weakness was political, not technical: it sat in committee and never came to a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2023, read twice, and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 9, 2023 and read twice, which is the standard first step in the Senate.
That same day it was referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action appears in the record — no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil companies and fuel sellers, who face no new federal anti-gouging penalties during emergencies; the price-gouging ban died before any vote.

for.name: Sen. Tammy Duckworth
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban unconscionably excessive gasoline prices during declared energy emergencies.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no recorded action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill received no Republican cosponsors and no recorded committee or floor action.

industries.note: During declared emergencies they could face civil penalties of up to triple profits or $100 million and criminal fines up to $500 million for unconscionably excessive prices. Enforcement priority would go to companies with over $10 billion in annual fuel sales.

Retail stations selling to motorists during an emergency could be sued by the FTC, the Justice Department, or state attorneys general for unconscionably excessive prices. Ordinary price changes reflecting real costs are expressly protected by the bill's factor list.
